• No analytics or crash-reporting SDK is built into this app.
• Engine logs stay in memory only and are wiped on disconnect.
• Settings never leave the device; there is no backend.
• App backup and cloud transfer of app data are disabled.
Local DoH, resolvers, speed test and the ECH lookup
Resolve names with DoH in the app
This app looks names up itself, over DoH, in every mode. The engine and the chain exit no longer resolve names for apps. Off = same as before. Applies on the next connect.
Add and save at least one resolver below, otherwise DoH stays off.
DoH resolvers (up to 3, tried in order)

Format: https://host/dns-query@address=IP. The IP is required, because ordinary DNS is never used to find the resolver. If every resolver fails, the connection fails: there is no fallback to normal DNS.
The resolver you chose sees the names, not the Tor exit. Off = with Tor the names are resolved at the Tor exit, as before.
Use expired answers when the resolver is unreachable
At most 10 minutes old. Nothing is refreshed in the background.
Names on your Direct list are also resolved by DoH, from your own network. Off (recommended): the phone\'s DNS is used, which domestic sites need.
Connect first: the test goes through the tunnel.
DoH is not active in the running connection (it was turned on after connecting, or Tor without “Also through Tor”). Reconnect to apply.
DoH works: a name was resolved and reached.
The tunnel works, but resolving a name through DoH failed. Check the resolver and its IP.
The tunnel itself is not carrying traffic right now.

Limits: apps with their own DoH/DoT, and Android\'s Private DNS, are not controlled. Names used over UDP (QUIC) are resolved by DoH too, because UDP goes through the app\'s own relay (with a Psiphon/Tor chain there is no UDP at all). IPv6 and HTTPS records are not answered. Proxy-only mode: only apps that send the NAME to the proxy (socks5h) use DoH. 100.64.0.0/10 is reserved for this feature while it is on.
Plain-IP resolvers, which is the only kind the engine understands. “Default” lets the engine use its own.
Not a plain IP, so it cannot be used: %1$s
Accepted: 1.1.1.1, 9.9.9.9:53, [2606:4700:4700::1111]:53. Names and DoH links are rejected here because the engine would silently ignore them.
Tests the entries above, or the built-in presets if the list is empty. It runs from your phone directly, not through the tunnel, so treat it as a hint.
Use udp://IP, tcp://IP or an https:// link (optionally with @address=IP).
Used only to fetch ECH keys. This is the one place the engine speaks DoH. Leave empty for the default.
Tunnel type, exit and what skips the tunnel
Per-app routing only works in VPN mode. In Proxy mode you choose apps yourself by pointing them at the proxy.
These go out over your real connection, not the tunnel: domestic sites, banks and anything that rejects foreign IPs. One rule per line: example.ir, full:host, keyword:word, 10.0.0.0/8.
These are refused outright and never reach the network. Good for ad and tracker lists.
Import a list file (txt, hosts, adblock)
No imported lists yet. Import a file or add a link: hosts files, AdGuard / adblock lists and plain domain lists all work.
Link to a list (https only). It is downloaded once; tap refresh to update it later. Nothing updates in the background.

Big lists are cleaned on import: comments, duplicates and entries already covered by a parent domain are dropped. Limits: 300,000 rules per list and 500,000 per tab (duplicates between lists count once). More rules mean more memory and a slower start.
This link is already in the list.
No usable rules found in this file.
The list is larger than 40 MB.
Tunnel everything EXCEPT the selected apps
Every app uses the tunnel. Change the mode above to pick exceptions.
Kept in memory only, never written to disk, and wiped when you disconnect. After an unexpected stop, a short redacted tail is kept in Diagnostics until you clear it.
Pick WireGuard, MASQUE or Gool above to chain Psiphon or Tor behind it. Smart mode cannot be chained.
Send your traffic through Psiphon or Tor after the WARP tunnel. Your network only sees WARP, and the exit country comes from Psiphon or Tor instead of WARP.

Choose where Psiphon should exit. Automatic lets Psiphon pick. First connect takes up to two extra minutes while it fetches a server list. Psiphon carries TCP only: website names are resolved at the exit and UDP apps (QUIC, calls) will not work.
Tor is slow and its first start can take up to five extra minutes while it downloads the network consensus. TCP only: website names are resolved at the exit and UDP apps (QUIC, calls) will not work.
Removed %1$d saved WARP identity file(s). A new one is registered on the next connect.
Use this if the exit IP stays stuck on an unwanted country. It deletes the saved WARP accounts; new ones are made on the next connect.

Carries Gool\'s outer MASQUE tunnel over TCP instead of QUIC. Use it when HTTP/3 never connects; on networks that throttle UDP it is usually the only one that works. If it is off and HTTP/3 fails, the app tries HTTP/2 by itself before falling back to classic Gool.

Balanced and Light use smaller buffers and a capped network scan, so the phone runs cooler and the battery lasts longer. Auto lets the core pick the biggest profile on a fast phone. Takes effect on the next connect.
Connection lost. Waiting to try again (about %1$d min), or sooner if the network changes.
No network. The engine is paused and starts again when the network returns.

Send your traffic through your own server after the WARP tunnel. Paste a vless://, vmess://, trojan:// or ss:// link; the app converts it for the built-in sing-box. The link is stored encrypted and never leaves this phone. XHTTP, mKCP and Shadowsocks plugins are not supported. TCP only: website names are resolved at your server and UDP apps (QUIC, calls) will not work.
Paste and save a link, or this chain cannot start.
The link could not be saved: this phone\'s secure storage (Keystore) is not working.
This kind of link is not supported. Supported: vless://, vmess://, trojan://, ss://.
The link has no valid port.
The link has no valid user id or password.
XHTTP is not supported by the official sing-box. Use a link with ws, grpc, httpupgrade or tcp.
This security setting is not supported.
VLESS encryption other than none is not supported.
Your custom link is not carrying traffic
No WARP endpoint could be reached. The engine is stopped and retries with growing pauses.
Remove IPs and keys when copying
Private addresses are hidden, public ones keep only their first two numbers, and tokens and keys are removed.

The kill switch only works while this app is running and covers the apps this VPN captures. Apps you excluded, apps that bypass VPNs on purpose, and some system services (carrier features such as Wi-Fi calling, work-profile apps) can still connect directly. Changes to app rules apply after a reconnect.

The only protection that also covers the moments before this app starts or after Android stops it is Android\'s own: open the VPN settings, choose this app, and turn on Always-on VPN and Block connections without VPN.

Under each app: whether it goes through the VPN, connects directly, or cannot be confirmed right now. Confirmed means the rule is part of the running VPN, not that an app can never find another route.
Adds system services and packages without an icon, such as Google Play services.
This app always connects directly (it carries the tunnel itself)
Cannot be confirmed in proxy mode: an app uses the proxy only if it is set up to

What is wrong, how sure we are, and the evidence
These are probabilities from measurements, not certainties. Run the tests below for firmer answers.
Samples every 3 seconds while this page is open. Off by default.
Measuring… the first figures appear in a few seconds.
Traffic rate is not available in proxy mode.
High CPU is only a problem when it does not match the traffic. The findings above say which one it is.
Opens a few short test connections through the tunnel and one outside it. Runs only when you press the button.
Kept in memory only, with IPs and keys removed, so the cause survives a restart. Cleared when you disconnect or tap Clear.
The report holds counters, states and the findings with their evidence. It never contains IP addresses, tokens or traffic content.
Include the end of the log
Off by default. When on, the last lines are added after IPs and keys are removed.
The engine process that carries the tunnel has stopped. Check Last unexpected stop below for the reason, then reconnect.
Connections by IP work but names are not being resolved. Try another resolver in the DNS tab.
The tunnel does not open connections. If the direct test works, the problem is the engine or the protocol, so try another protocol. If it fails too, the network itself is down.
The engine cannot complete its handshake or find a working gateway on this network. Try another protocol, Gool over HTTP/2, or a different scan mode.
The tunnel is up but data stopped
Apps are sending but nothing comes back. A reconnect usually fixes it; if it keeps happening, the exit or this network is dropping the tunnel.
Several reconnects in a short time. Try another protocol, and check whether the network changes (Wi-Fi to mobile) around the drops.
High CPU because of real traffic
The engine is busy because data is really flowing. This is expected; it ends when the transfer does.

The engine uses a lot of CPU without matching traffic. Likely causes are listed in the evidence: a Psiphon/Tor chain, repeated reconnects or a heavy performance profile. Try the Light profile in Settings.
In proxy mode the traffic rate cannot be measured, so real use cannot be told apart from idle burning. Compare with how much you are actually using the proxy.
Nothing in the measurements points to a fault. If something still fails, run the tests for a firmer answer.

Sends fewer keep-alive and health packets and waits longer before it calls a quiet tunnel dead. Less radio use and fewer needless reconnects; a real outage is noticed up to about 30 seconds later. Takes effect at the next connect.
\"Only selected apps\" is on but no app is selected (or the selected apps are gone). Select at least one app, or switch the mode off.
Shows upload and download speed in the status notification, like sing-box. Updates only while the screen is on, so it costs nothing in your pocket. VPN mode only.
Psiphon and Tor need a fixed protocol. If Smart was selected, it is switched to MASQUE (HTTP/2); change it in Settings if you prefer another.
The new profile is used the next time you connect.
Iranian IP ranges (v2ray geoip.dat). Only the Iran entries are read.
Iranian websites (v2ray geosite.dat). Only the Iran entries are read.
Ads, trackers and malware. Balanced, few false alarms.
Ads, trackers and malware. Large list.

The core\'s own Chrome-like handshake. Nothing is changed.
Adds the four extras Chrome sends (GREASE signature algorithm, brotli certificate compression, ALPS, ECH GREASE). The first packet keeps its size.
Sends Firefox\'s handshake instead: a post-quantum key share and its own cipher and signature order. The first packet is about 1.2 KB larger.
Not a valid domain name. An IP address is not allowed; use a name such as example.com.
The server name is used only by the MASQUE protocols. The protocol chosen now does not use it.

Worth changing only when MASQUE over HTTP/2 is blocked while WireGuard or HTTP/3 still work. Only the first handshake packet changes, so it costs no battery. The server name is the one sent in the clear in every MASQUE handshake: Default is www.cloudflare.com, and WARP client is what Cloudflare\'s own app sends. The TLS look also covers the calls to the WARP API; Zero Trust sign-in keeps its own TLS. Applies on the next connect.

The Kill Switch works only while this app is running. If Android stops the app (low memory, force stop), traffic can leave unprotected. For full protection turn on Always-on VPN and Block connections without VPN for MadShield in Android\'s VPN settings.
Warning: this link turns certificate checking off (allowInsecure). Anyone between you and the server could read or change the traffic. Use it only if you know why it is needed.

On (default): UDP is carried through the tunnel (voice and video calls, games, QUIC) and your block/direct rules are applied to every UDP packet too. Off: no UDP is sent at all; TCP, the VPN and the Kill Switch are not affected. Applied at once while the app\'s routing front runs, otherwise at the next connect.
With UDP off, names are answered by the app\'s own DNS (IPv4 only) and travel over TCP. Apps that need UDP (calls, QUIC) will not work.
Psiphon and Tor carry TCP only, so UDP is refused while one of them is the chain. Use a custom (sing-box) chain whose server supports UDP.
Blocked by rule %1$d, guard %2$d, malformed %3$d, no upstream/lookup %4$d, queue full %5$d
Connect to see what UDP is doing.
No counters: no routing front runs, so the VPN talks UDP to the upstream itself.
On: rules apply to every packet
On: straight to the upstream (no rules to apply)
Refused: this chain carries TCP only

Turns off at the next connect
What carries the phone\'s traffic into the tunnel
The engine of every earlier version. Nothing is changed.
EXPERIMENTAL: sing-box 1.15 with its new TCP/IP stack, in its own process. It forwards to the same local port as hev, so DNS, routing rules, chains and the Kill Switch work as before.
This build has no sing-box TUN engine. Connecting will fail with that reason until you choose hev.
Applies at the next connection: disconnect and connect again. If the engine cannot start, the reason is shown; it never switches back to hev by itself.
Scan, noise, MTU, TLS, tunnel engine
Animation runs only while the app is on screen and stops completely in the background, so it never uses battery.
Open connections, their route, close any of them

The list is available while the VPN is connected and the app\'s routing is on (routing rules, a privacy chain, DNS-over-HTTPS or UDP off). Names are kept in memory only and vanish when you disconnect.

Your WARP identity, rule lists, settings and usage totals are never removed.
MadShield shows the connection status (and speed, if you want) in a notification. Without it you cannot see or stop the VPN from the notification shade.
Let it run in the background
Android can put the VPN to sleep when the screen is off, which drops the connection. Allowing this keeps it running; MadShield still uses very little battery.
Restricted: Android may stop the VPN in the background

Shows the status on the lock screen and as a chip in the status bar. With Speed in notification on, the download speed shows in the chip and both speeds on the lock screen. Android decides when to show it, and you can turn it off for this app in Android settings.
Live updates are off for this app in Android settings

Mozilla\'s VPN through your own Firefox Account, as a separate engine next to WARP (not chained with it). Your traffic goes from this phone straight to Mozilla\'s servers. One account, with its own free monthly data (about 50 GB). This is an unofficial client: Mozilla has not approved it.

Your Firefox password and sign-in tokens stay in this app\'s private folder on this phone. Mozilla\'s proxy carries TCP only, so UDP is off with this engine. MadShield uses one account and never switches between accounts, because Mozilla\'s terms allow one account per person.

If the speed drops to a few KB/s while it still connects, your network may be slowing every connection down on its own. More parallel sessions spread your connections over several of them; HTTP/3 uses UDP instead of TCP, which some networks treat differently. Try one change at a time and test the speed; 1 and HTTP/2 stay the default because more sessions cost a little more battery.

If sign-in or connecting stops with “TLS handshake timeout”, a filter on your network is probably reading the server name. Splitting the first packet often gets past it, and Mozilla\'s servers receive the same bytes. It applies to sign-in and to the connection.
A connection is running: the choice applies at the next connection.
Not a usable address: it must start with https:// and name a domain (no IP address, no ? or #).

Only if Foxy fails with \'Guardian does not serve this region\' (HTTP 451): Mozilla refuses the region of your own address. A relay is a small Cloudflare Worker that you deploy yourself (tools/guardian-relay in the source); the account\'s pass requests then leave from its address. The relay sees your Firefox Account access token, so use only your own, never someone else\'s. Leave it empty for the normal direct connection.
Mozilla\'s bot check refuses a password sent from the app (“HTTP 406”). Its own sign-in page, shown here in a browser engine, passes it. Nothing you type is kept by the app.

Asked from inside the app\'s own tunnel (Cloudflare\'s trace page, by address, so no name lookup is made). Your real IP is never shown here.

When the timer ends it is an ordinary Disconnect: the Kill Switch lets go too, so normal internet returns. In deep sleep Android may run it a few minutes late.
